g.text: COMPLEX NUMBERS, POLAR/EULER GEOMETRY & ARGAND DOMAIN TOPOLOGY ENGINE
Cartesian-Polar Duality // Euler Identities // Triangle Inequalities // Roots of Unity Polygons // Domain Topology
Rectangular, Polar, and Exponential representations with conjugate reflection
Rectangular (Cartesian): z = x + i y = Re(z) + i Im(z)
• Real axis: x = Re(z) = (z + z̄)/2 | Imaginary axis: y = Im(z) = (z - z̄)/(2i)
Polar / Trigonometric: z = r (cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ
Exponential (Euler): z = r eᵢṤ where eᵢṤ = cos θ + i sin θ
• Compact multiplication: z₁ z₂ = r₁ r₂ eᵢ(θ₁+θ₂) | Division: z₁/z₂ = (r₁/r₂) eᵢ(θ₁-θ₂)
• Quad II (x<0, y≥0): θ = π - tan⁻¹(|y/x|)
Conjugate Reflection: z̄ = x - i y = r e⁻ᵢṤ
• Reflection across real axis: |z̄| = |z|, Arg(z̄) = -Arg(z) (for z ∉ ℝ⁻)
• Core Identity: z · z̄ = |z|² = x² + y² (always non-negative real)
POWERS OF IOTA & CIRCULAR-HYPERBOLIC INTERLINKING FORMULAS
★ For any k ∈ ℤ: i⁴ᵐ = 1, i⁴ᵐ⁺¹ = i, i⁴ᵐ⁺² = -1, i⁴ᵐ⁺³ = -i
⚠ sin z and cos z are NOT bounded in ℂ!
Parallelogram law of addition // Distance metric // Absolute extrema bounds
• Equality holds iff arg(z₁) = arg(z₂) (vectors are collinear & codirectional)
• Equality holds iff arg(z₁) = arg(z₂) (same direction, subtracting)
GATE PARADIGM: EXTREMA OF |z + w| ON A CIRCLE
Given: |z| = R (circle of radius R centered at origin)
Find maximum and minimum values of |z + z₀| where z₀ is a fixed point.
Occurs when z and z₀ point in the exact same direction.
Occurs when z and z₀ point in opposite directions.
PARALLELOGRAM EQUALITY & DE MOIVRE'S POWER EXPANSION THEOREM
• Sum of squares of diagonal lengths = Sum of squares of all 4 side lengths
★ Crucial GATE shortcut for finding unknown diagonal when side lengths & one diagonal are given!
[r (cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ (cos nθ + i sin nθ)
• Holds for all integers n ∈ ℤ (positive, zero, and negative)
• For fractional n = p/q: yields q distinct roots spaced uniformly around circle
★ Euler equivalent: (eᵢṤ)ⁿ = eᵢⁿṤ. Simplifies polynomial trigonometric expansions.
03. N-TH ROOTS OF UNITY & POLYGONAL SYMMETRY
Roots equation zⁿ = 1 // Geometric distribution // Fundamental sum and product identities
zⁿ = 1 = eᵢ²ᵐᵖ ⇒ ωₖ = eᵢ(²ᵐᵖ/ⁿ), k = 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1
• Vertices of a regular n-gon inscribed inside unit circle |z| = 1.
• Angle between consecutive roots: Δθ = 2π / n.
★ Fundamental Properties: 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1
★ 1 + ωᵒ + ω²ᵒ = 3 (if r is multiple of 3) else 0
• Vertices of a square centered at origin with edge length √2
Sum of all n roots = ∑ᵏ₌₀ ωᵏ = 0 (for any n ≥ 2)
Product of all n roots = ∏ᵏ₌₀ ωᵏ = (-1)ⁿ⁻¹
• Geometric proof: Centroid of regular n-gon is exactly at origin (0,0)
★ For cube roots: (1 - ω)(1 - ω²) = 1 - (ω+ω²) + ω³ = 1 - (-1) + 1 = 3
★ Repeatedly tested in GATE for product evaluations without manual angles!
Let c = R eᵢϕ. Then: zᵏ = R¹/ⁿ eᵢ((ϕ + 2kπ)/n)
• Magnitude of all roots is identical: |zᵏ| = R¹/ⁿ = |c|¹/ⁿ
• Roots form a regular polygon rotated by phase ϕ/n
Roots: 2(1±i)/√2, 2(-1±i)/√2 = ±√2 ± i√2 (all 4 lie on circle radius 2)
Neighborhoods // Interior & Boundary Points // Simply vs Multiply Connected Domains
δ-Neighborhood (Open Disk): Nδ(z₀) = {z ∈ ℂ : |z - z₀| < δ}
Interior Point: ∃ δ>0 such that Nδ(z₀) ⊂ S
Boundary Point: Every Nδ(z₀) intersects both S and Sᶜ
Open Set: Every point of S is an interior point
Closed Set: Contains all its boundary points (S̄ = S)
An open set D is a Domain if it is connected (any two points can be joined by a polygonal path inside D).
• Every simple closed curve C lying entirely in D can be contracted to a point without leaving D.
• The interior of C contains ONLY points belonging to D.
★ Required condition for Cauchy-Goursat theorem: ∮ᶜ f(z) dz = 0!
• Domain has one or more "holes" or excluded singular points.
• An annulus r₁ < |z - z₀| < r₂ has 1 hole (doubly connected).
★ Requires cross-cuts or Laurent series rather than single Taylor expansion!
|z - z₀| = R ⇒ Circle center z₀, rad R
⇒ Perpendicular bisector of segment joining z₁ and z₂
Re(z) = c ⇒ Vertical line x = c
Im(z) = c ⇒ Horizontal line y = c
Arg(z) = θ₀ ⇒ Ray emanating from origin
• If k ≠ 1: True Circle (Circle of Apollonius)
• Frequently tested in Bilinear mapping boundary problems in GATE EC & EE!
